newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany set guidelines for asset-backed deals - Buba.
newsitem.headline: Germany set guidelines for asset-backed deals - Buba.

text.p: Germany's banking watchdog has issued guidelines for the use of asset-backed securities (ABS) but it remains to be seen to what extent German banks will make use of such transactions, which are well established in other countries, the Bundesbank said on Wednesday.

The Federal Banking Supervisory Office this year issued the guidelines in response to calls from German banks for some form of regulation of ABS transactions, the Bundesbank said in its July monthly report.
In such a transaction a bank sells part of its loan portfolio to a company which finances the purchase by issuing debt in the form of asset backed securities.

The initial advantage for the bank is that it obtains liquidity and can earn risk-free commission income, but the full benefit of such transactions is only achieved if the bank removes the loans from its balance sheet, thereby increasing its scope to extend fresh credit, the Bundesbank said.

The guidelines, which determine whether banks can use ABS deals to ease their balance sheets, were issued because the European Union is unlikely to provide harmonised regulation on ABS in the near future, the Bundesbank said.
They are aimed at preventing the sale of bank loans leading to a deterioration of the bank's remaining loan portfolio.
The Supervisory Office in 1990 voiced objections to an ABS transaction by the German subsidiary of an international banking group, the Bundesbank said.
The Office had said it was concerned that such transactions meant banks could be bypassed and lose their status as mediators between debtors and investors.
Also, the relationship of trust between the customer and his banker could be damaged if the customer's debt was passed to another creditor without his approval.
But experience in the U.S. and other countries showed there had been virtually no case to date in which an ABS transaction had failed, the bank said.

That was because ABS were generally regarded as secure and relatively successful investment vehicles and because the transactions tended to be carried out by large, reputable institutions, the Bundesbank said.
